passage: Rashmi, you asked how I cope at prayer time with Dadi when I'm unsure about half of it. Let me tell you what I did at fifteen. I'm Jeevan, and I had stopped believing in some of the rituals. Every evening Dadi lit the lamp and sang, and I sat beside her with my shoes off. I didn't mock. I didn't pretend either; inside, I stayed honest. Once she asked, "Do you believe like me?" I said, "Not the same way, Dadi, but I love sitting here with you." She patted my knee and kept singing. Years later I remember her songs better than most lessons.

qa.q: How old was Jeevan when this happened?
What was Jeevan feeling as Jeevan sat beside Dadi?
qa.a: Love for Dadi together with honest doubt inside; Jeevan stayed beside Dadi but did not pretend to believe everything.

qa.q: How can someone with doubts still honour a grandparent's faith?
qa.a: Sit beside the grandparent, listen, do not mock, and be gently honest if asked, as Jeevan did.

qa.q: How might Dadi have felt when Jeevan said "Not the same way"?
qa.a: Perhaps a little sad, but also comforted by the love; she patted Jeevan's knee and kept singing.

grounding: Jeevan loses belief in some rituals but sits beside the grandmother at prayer out of love while staying honest inside.

passage:
"Ira, aarti time," Nani called from the prayer corner.

Ira put down her phone and went. Her cousin Neelam, visiting for the holidays, followed, smirking.

Afterwards, on the terrace, Neelam said, "You know you don't believe that stuff. You told me last month. So why do you sit there every evening like a good girl?"

"Because Nani likes it when I sit with her."

"But it's fake if you don't believe."

Ira thought. "I don't think the lamp does anything. I've stopped thinking that. But Nani's hands shake now when she holds the plate. She sings off-key and she doesn't care. Sitting there is how I'm with her."

"So you're pretending."

"I'm not pretending to believe. If she asks, I'll tell her. I'm just not going to make fun of something that holds her up."

Neelam was quiet. Then, "Can I sit with you both tomorrow?"

"Only if you don't laugh."

qa.q: Where did Nani call Ira from?
qa.a: Nani called Ira from the prayer corner.

qa.q: What does Ira feel when she sits beside Nani at aarti?
qa.a: Ira feels tender love for Nani, noticing her shaking hands and off-key singing, even without believing in the ritual.

qa.q: What did Ira do that was wise in answering Neelam?
qa.a: Ira was honest about her doubts, said she would tell Nani if asked, and refused to mock something that holds Nani up.

qa.q: How might Nani feel having Ira beside her every evening?
qa.a: Nani probably feels loved and less alone, glad to share the evening with her granddaughter.

grounding: It shows a teen who has lost belief in a ritual but still sits beside her grandmother at prayer out of love, staying honest inside and refusing to mock her faith.

passage:
Every Thursday evening, my Ammamma walks to the small Sai temple at the end of our street in Chennai, and every Thursday, I go with her. I'm Urmila, and somewhere in Class 10 I stopped believing most of it.

It didn't happen in one day. I just started finding the rituals empty: the coconut, the bell, the same prayer every week. Once, my friend Mehak asked me, "If you don't believe, why go? Isn't that fake?"

I thought about it for days. Then I realised: I go for Ammamma. She holds my arm on the uneven road. She tells me which aunty's son got married. Inside, she closes her eyes and her face goes soft in a way I never see at home.

I don't fold my hands the way she does anymore. I don't pretend when she asks what I prayed for; I say, "For you, Ammamma." That's true.

And I never, ever laugh at her. It isn't mine to take away.

qa.q: Where does Ammamma go every Thursday evening?
qa.a: Ammamma walks to the small Sai temple at the end of the street.

qa.q: What does Urmila feel while walking with Ammamma?
qa.a: Urmila feels a warm, protective affection for Ammamma, even though the rituals now feel empty.

qa.q: How does Urmila stay honest while still honouring Ammamma?
qa.a: Urmila no longer folds hands as Ammamma does and answers truthfully that the prayer is for Ammamma, while never mocking her faith.

qa.q: What might Mehak think after hearing Urmila's reasons?
qa.a: Mehak might see that going to the temple can be about love for a person, not only about belief.

grounding: It shows a teen who loses belief in some rituals but still sits beside Ammamma at prayer out of love, honouring her while staying honest inside.
